seoTitle: Triangle angle Calculator: Free, With Steps
seoDesc: Triangle angle: work out angle α from the side length b and the side length c. A free math calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Triangle angle calculator turns the side length b, the side length c and the angle α into angle α. That makes it useful for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. Change one value and the results step aside until you press Calculate again, which is what makes it easy to see how much the answer really depends on that one input.

sections.title: How does the Triangle angle calculator work?
sections.html:
The Triangle angle calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports angle α in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the given and the angle selection); then you type in the side length b, the side length c, the angle α (2) and the side length a (2).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Triangle angle calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Angle α=(((1 ÷ 2) × (-(side length a ^ 2) + (side length b ^ 2) + (side length c ^ 2)) ÷ (side length b × side length c)))
Angle β=(((1 ÷ 2) × ((side length a ^ 2) − (side length b ^ 2) + (side length c ^ 2)) ÷ (side length a × side length c)))
Angle γ=(((1 ÷ 2) × ((side length a ^ 2) + (side length b ^ 2) − (side length c ^ 2)) ÷ (side length a × side length b)))
Side length b=side length c × the cosine of (angle α) + the square root of ((side length a ^ 2) − (side length c ^ 2) × (the sine of (angle α), 2))
Angle β=((1 ÷ 2) × ((side length a ^ 2) − (side length b ^ 2) + (side length c ^ 2)) ÷ (side length a × side length c))
Side length a=side length b × the cosine of (angle γ) + the square root of (-(side length b ^ 2) × (the sine of (angle γ), 2) + (side length c ^ 2))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Given set to angle and 2 sides, Angle selection set to α, Side length a = 30 cm and Side length b = 30 cm. The calculator returns Angle α = 60 deg, Angle β = 60 deg and Angle γ = 60 deg.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Angle α = 60 deg, Angle β = 60 deg and Angle γ = 60 deg should be roughly the size you expected from Given set to angle and 2 sides and Angle selection set to α.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Triangle angle calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the side length b, the side length c and the angle α — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Triangle angle calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns angle α, derived from the side length b, the side length c and the angle α. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Triangle angle calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the side length b, the side length c and the angle α, which is 16 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter side length a in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Side length a opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Angle α = 60 deg. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Triangle angle calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
